scenes.text: In 1977, you could fly from London to New York in about three and a half hours.
Today, the same trip takes around seven or eight.
And that isn't just the story of one unusual plane. The ordinary jets got stuck too.
The Boeing 747 entered service in 1970. It cruised at about eighty-five percent of the speed of sound.
The newest airliners flying today cruise at... about eighty-five percent of the speed of sound.
In those fifty-odd years, computers went from filling rooms to fitting in pockets. The speed of a passenger jet barely moved.
So what happened? Did we forget how to build fast planes?
No. We hit a wall. And the wall is made of air.
A wing works partly by speeding up the air that flows over its top. That air moves faster than the plane itself.
So when the plane flies at about eighty percent of the speed of sound, parts of the air on top of the wing are already going faster than sound.
And where that supersonic air has to slow down again, it forms a shock wave.
Shock waves are expensive. They add a whole new kind of drag, and it doesn't creep up gently. Past a certain speed, it shoots up.
For many airliners, that steep rise begins somewhere between eighty and eighty-five percent of the speed of sound.
Just where the 747 flew in 1970. And just where airliners fly now.
And drag isn't just a number in a wind tunnel. It's paid for in fuel.
More drag means the engines have to push harder. Pushing harder means burning more fuel for every kilometre.
And fuel is one of the biggest bills an airline pays. Often a quarter to a third of everything it spends.
So airlines don't simply fly as fast as their planes can go. They choose a speed that balances the cost of fuel against the cost of time.
Too slow, and the crew is paid for longer, and the plane fits fewer trips into a day.
Too fast, and fuel costs climb sharply. Airlines look for the balance.
Even some versions of the Boeing 707, back in the 1960s, could fly at up to ninety percent of the speed of sound. Airlines usually flew it at about eighty-two.
Engineers did find ways to push the wall back a little. Swept-back wings. And in the 1960s, at NASA, Richard Whitcomb's supercritical wing.
It could have been used to fly faster. Mostly, airliners used it to fly at the same speed on less fuel.
Remember that choice. It's going to keep coming back.
Because somebody did try to fly faster, right up at the wall. In 1962, the Convair 990 entered service as the fastest airliner in the world.
But it never quite reached the speed it had been promised. And it burned more fuel than the Boeing 707.
For the airlines, a little extra speed wasn't worth the fuel. Only thirty-seven were ever built.
So flying just a little faster at the wall doesn't pay. But what about going straight through it?
That's Concorde. It cruised at twice the speed of sound, over two thousand kilometres an hour.
Getting through the wall didn't make the wall go away. It just meant paying for it.
Concorde carried about a hundred people. Per passenger, it burned roughly three times as much fuel as a 747.
And it brought something no ordinary airliner makes. A sonic boom.
A sonic boom isn't a single bang at the moment you pass the speed of sound. It follows the plane the whole way, a carpet of noise on the ground dozens of kilometres wide.
In 1973, the United States banned civilian supersonic flight over its land. And Concorde was kept mostly to routes over the sea.
That left it a handful of routes, mostly London and Paris to New York. Only twenty were ever built.
And its timing was terrible. Concorde was designed in the 1960s, when fuel was cheap.
In early 1973, the big American airlines that had held options on it pulled out. Then, that October, the oil crisis sent fuel prices soaring. Two separate blows, a few months apart.
In 1997, a return ticket from New York to London cost over eight thousand dollars.
Some people paid it. Not enough of them. Concorde had always been expensive to run and to maintain.
After a crash in 2000, and a slump in air travel after September 2001, it flew its last passengers in 2003.
So now we know where the wall is, and what it costs to get past it.
But the clearest answer came in the early 2000s. Because then, the airlines got something very close to a direct choice.
In 2001, Boeing proposed the Sonic Cruiser. It would fly just under the speed of sound, at up to ninety-eight percent of it. Around fifteen to twenty percent faster than a normal airliner.
By 2002, Boeing was also discussing another idea with airlines. A plane that flew at the usual speed, but burned seventeen to twenty percent less fuel than a 767.
Faster... or cheaper.
Cheaper won. In 2002, Boeing dropped the Sonic Cruiser and turned to efficiency instead. That plane became the Boeing 787.
It's the same choice Whitcomb's wing ran into. The same trade-off that hurt the Convair, and that Concorde never escaped.
Again and again, airlines chose efficiency over speed.
Which makes it sound like airliners stood still for fifty years. They didn't.
They just got better at something else.
A new airliner today uses about half as much fuel per seat, for the same distance, as a new one from the 1960s.
And over those years, flying got much cheaper.
In the United States, the median domestic return fare, adjusted for inflation, fell by almost forty percent between 1980 and 2005.
And air travel exploded. In 1970, the world's airlines carried a few hundred million passengers. Before the pandemic, it was four and a half billion a year.
So planes did get faster. Just not between the airports.
In 1970, flying abroad was still beyond the budget of many ordinary families. Over the decades, that changed. Flying became affordable to far more people.
We were watching the wrong number. Speed is the one you can see on the departures board. Price is the one that decided who got on the plane at all.
But that bargain might be about to change.
NASA's X-59 is built to make a much quieter sonic boom. Its whole shape is designed to spread the shock waves out, so on the ground, it should sound more like a distant thump.
In 2026, it flew faster than sound for the first time.
And in 2026, the American regulator proposed replacing the ban over land with a limit on how loud the boom can be on the ground. It's a proposal, not yet a rule.
A start-up called Boom Supersonic is designing an airliner for that world, with a first flight planned for the late 2020s.
But notice what hasn't changed. Getting past the wall still costs more fuel.
So the old question is still there. Not whether we can build it. We could in the 1970s. But who pays for the hours it saves.
For fifty years, most of us chose the cheaper seat. And we got what we chose.
Planes no faster than the ones from 1970... carrying more than ten times as many passengers a year.
So here's a question for you. How much would you pay to land three hours earlier? Let me know in the comments.
